passage: "Jagdish, you think your Nani was always good with numbers? When I was ten, the maths teacher in our Indore school said in front of everyone, 'Girls, don't worry, sums are not for you. Just pass.' I had done every sum at home. But on test day I felt a knot, here, in my stomach. I kept thinking, 'Don't prove him right, Preeti. Don't prove him right.' I read the first question four times. The numbers slid about like ants. I left half the paper blank. That evening I solved the same paper at home in twenty minutes. The sums had not changed; only the voice in my head had gone quiet. Only a kind teacher in Class 7 made me believe it again."

qa.a: Jagdish may see that a poor result can come from pressure and a label, not a lack of ability, and that a kind word can change it.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how a teacher's remark that sums are not for girls knotted her stomach during a test and crowded out answers she knew.

passage: Hemant, ten, had moved from the municipal school to the big school across the flyover in Thane in June. On the first day Omkar told him cheerfully, "Municipal kids are always weak in English, na? Don't feel bad." Hemant had read three storybooks that month. But on Friday, when the teacher said, "Dictation, twenty words," a knot formed in his stomach. He felt Omkar's eyes on his notebook. 'Receive.' Was it ie or ei? He knew this. He wrote it, rubbed it out, wrote it again. By the time he looked up, the teacher was on word nine. He had missed three. Walking home, he spelled 'receive' perfectly in his head, which made it worse.

qa.a: Feeling Omkar's eyes and remembering the remark about municipal kids, he was so afraid of proving it true that he doubted a word he knew.

qa.q: How might Omkar read Hemant's dictation mark, and why would that be misleading?
qa.a: Omkar might think the low mark proves the remark, not realising the fear of being judged is what made Hemant miss the words.

grounding: A boy from a municipal school, told such children are weak in English, feels a knot in his stomach during dictation and misses words he knows.

subtype: Feeling watched for a group label [Actor]
passage:
I'm Nandini. Last year, when I was eleven, Trisha and I were the only girls in the mental-maths round at the inter-school fest. At home I could add big numbers in my head faster than my dad.
Just before we went up, a boy from the other team said loudly, "Girls always freeze in speed rounds." His friends giggled. The quizmaster read the first question, and my stomach twisted into a knot. All I could hear was his voice. I got the first three wrong, even the easy one.
Trisha squeezed my hand under the table. On the fourth question I shut my eyes and pictured our kitchen table. I got it.
Now I know the numbers never left me. The worry was just sitting on top of them.

qa.q: What did the boy from the other team say?
qa.a: He said, 'Girls always freeze in speed rounds.'

qa.q: Why did Nandini get the first three questions wrong, even the easy one?
qa.a: Her stomach knotted and all she could hear was the boy's voice, so the fear of proving him right crowded out the numbers.

qa.q: What helped Nandini get the fourth question right?
qa.a: Trisha's squeeze and picturing the kitchen table at home calmed her enough for her real skill to come back.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt watching Nandini miss easy questions?
qa.a: Trisha may have felt worried and protective, knowing how good Nandini is, which is why she squeezed her hand.

grounding: A girl told that girls freeze in speed rounds feels a knot and misses easy questions, as fear of the label uses up her mental space.
